title: Why Holiday Travel Brings More Crashes and Delays: 81.5 Million Thanksgiving Travelers, Explained

beats.text: AAA expects 81.5 million Americans to travel fifty miles or more this Thanksgiving. About 73 million will drive, and roughly 6 million will fly.

That's slightly fewer than last year's record, partly because travel costs more. But the roads and airports will still be packed. So why does holiday travel bring more crashes and delays? Here are the three big reasons.

overlays.sub: partly due to higher travel costs

beats.text: One: too many cars, not enough road. Every highway has a limit. Close to it, one driver taps the brakes, the car behind brakes harder, and a wave of red lights rolls backwards. Engineers call it a phantom jam. And in stop-and-go traffic, short gaps and sudden braking make rear-end crashes more likely.

Two: tired drivers on unfamiliar roads. Many people drive for hours after a full workday, often after dark, on routes they don't know, sometimes in rain or snow. And when you're running late, it's tempting to speed and tailgate.

Three: airports have almost no slack. Airlines schedule each plane for several flights a day, back to back. If one flight leaves late, the next flight on that plane is late too, and so are its crew and passengers.
It's a domino effect. A storm or a backup at one busy hub can ripple delays across the country within hours.
So what can you do? Leave early in the morning, or travel on quieter days. Rest before a long drive and take breaks. Keep a bigger gap, and give yourself extra time at the airport.
Are you driving or flying this Thanksgiving? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who's about to hit the road. Because 81.5 million Americans are about to share the same roads and skies.
